transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-12
Start time: 11:00 AM EDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Julian Park (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Redwood CSM), Leah Chen (NovaCommerce SRE), Marcus Rivera (Lead ML Eng), Rogan Patel (CTO), Ivy Gomez (PM)

Auto-summary (auto): recurring 5xxs at p99 tail, intermittent client timeouts, missing KV cache miss counters in customer instrumentation, action items set for logs and synthetic test.

[00:00] Ava: okay everyone thanks for joining the weekly POC sync, uh we'll try to keep to 45 minutes, we've got a few follow ups from last week's incident, Julian is going to run through what we found on our side and then Leah and Marcus can share their environment notes
[00:18] Julian: yeah thanks Ava, um quick context — we took the traces from the window you flagged Friday 05-08, and we see a cluster of 5xxs that line up with higher than normal input token sizes plus concurrent bursts from two microservices, so two things colliding basically
[00:36] Marcus: hi Julian, Marcus here. when you say concurrent bursts, is that at the load balancer level or is it internal queuing on the Redwood runtime?
[00:48] Julian: good question. from the traces we have, the request reaches the LB fine then we see a short queuing delay on the cluster node, and then a timeout from the client after about 18s. some of the 5xxs are internal 502/504s and others look like gateway timeouts. transcription note: a couple of proper nouns got fuzzy in the auto transcript (kv cache -> K-V cash) so I'm clarifying live
[01:12] Leah: and to add — our side saw simultaneous retries from the business service when latency spiked, so that multiplied the pressure. we don't have a clear metric for kvcache miss rate in our instrumentation, we only track cache hits at a coarse level
[01:30] Ava: oh that's an important telemetry gap, ok Julian can you explain where KV cache metrics would show up and what to look for
[01:38] Julian: sure. in Redwood's runtime we emit kv_cache_hit, kv_cache_miss, prefix_cache_lookup_time. those are in the agent logs and we can expose them to your monitoring if you want. right now the traces we got don't include kv_cache_miss counts, so we can't confirm whether cache misses drove the extra token compute
[01:56] Rogan: so if we're missing kv cache misses we might be underestimating token compute costs too, right? which affects scaling and cost planning
[02:06] Maya: correct. and also from a reliability POV if cache warmup isn't tracked you get blind tail latencies during cold windows
[02:16] Ivy: quick question — could the 5xxs be tied to model switchovers? we do have a canary set up that flips between gpt-like-2 and gpt-open-3 when latency thresholds cross
[02:28] Julian: we checked model rollout logs — there was a fallback event during the spike but it didn't coincide exactly with the first 5xx cluster. there was, however, a small GC activity spike on nodes around the same time, so it's potentially multi-factor
[02:40] Marcus: are you seeing any correlation with network egress or VPC bandwidth saturation? we run in a VPC with egress limits from our cloud provider
[02:50] Julian: we do not have your VPC flow logs in the set we analyzed. Leah?
[02:55] Leah: right we didn't attach those last week, my bad. I can pull the flow logs and egress throttle alerts from our provider and share them. there was a recent change to our egress QoS we forgot to mention
[03:06] Ava: okay please include that in the follow-up, could be critical. Julian, you mentioned gateway 502/504s — do you have example request IDs we can look at?
[03:16] Julian: yes I have a small set of request IDs, I'll attach them. the pattern is: heavy input, prefix cache missed, longer kernel selection, then timeout or 502. again the transcript may have garbled some kernel names (cuda -> cooda sometimes)
[03:28] Rogan: haha, fair. on the customer side we also saw client side timeouts at 18 to 20 seconds, our SDK default retry is 3 with exponential backoff. we might be contributing to the thundering retry pattern
[03:42] Ava: that's an important tradeoff — retry budget is useful but can amplify a transient backend problem. we should align on recommended retry/backoff settings for your use case
[03:52] Marcus: what's Redwood's recommended scheme for low-latency workloads? we care about p95 under 800ms but p99 matters for UI too
[04:02] Julian: for UI requests we suggest minimal retries (zero to one) and client timeout slightly under the server SLO so the server can surface an error. for async/batch usecases you can be more aggressive. we also have adaptive throttling options in Redwood Optimize — but that needs good telemetry enabling to be effective
[04:22] Ivy: can you explain adaptive throttling briefly?
[04:26] Julian: sure — it uses recent per-route queue lengths, token compute cost and observed tail latency to decide to shed low-priority requests and route to a cheaper model variant when capacity is saturated. but again it requires per-route metrics e.g. queue_length, token_cost_estimate, kv_cache_miss_rate to avoid wrong decisions
[04:44] Leah: ok so first practical ask from us is to send the flow logs and point us to where to enable kv cache metrics in our client agent
[04:52] Ava: agreed. second, Julian will send the example request IDs and a filtered trace bundle. third, we want NovaCommerce to run a synthetic baseline test — 10k tokens over 30 minutes at consistent RPS so we have a baseline for the environment.
[05:08] Marcus: can you propose the test payloads? we need to match real inputs to reproduce cache behavior
[05:13] Julian: yes, we'll share a small set of representative prompts, and include cold-start and hot-warm sequences to exercise the KV cache. we'll also include a version that ramps concurrent short requests to reproduce tail queuing.
[05:26] Rogan: one more thing — we've seen a config on our side that sets connection pooling by host to 5, maybe we need to increase that for burst windows
[05:35] Maya: good catch. there are a lot of knobs: client pooling, SDK retry, LB timeouts, Redwood's per-route concurrency and batching. let's list them and prioritize later in the notes
[05:48] Ivy: do we need a canary to test dedicated burst pool versus hosted? curious about cost vs reliability tradeoff
[05:56] Ava: yes we can scope a short pilot: 24-hour dedicated burst on a small pool to see if the 5xx rate drops under comparable load. I'll include pricing delta in the follow up.
[06:07] Leah: and while we're experimenting, can Redwood share a hop-by-hop latency export? we just want to see which hop is the biggest contributor at p99
[06:16] Julian: yes, we can emit per-token latency breakdown: LB -> ingress serialization -> model kernel selection -> token generation -> egress. we'll send a template CSV with the fields we can produce
[06:26] Marcus: perfect. regarding the earlier GC spike you mentioned, is there any control from Redwood to reduce service-side GC pressure?
[06:34] Julian: the runtime is managed by Redwood; we can change model shard sizing and kernel batching thresholds which impact memory churn, and we can recommend model quantization profiles that reduce working set. those are actions we'd coordinate with you during a maintenance window
[06:49] Rogan: we are also sensitive to compliance — any logs or traces shared must be redacted. can you confirm the export scrub process?
[06:56] Maya: yes we scrub PII and we can apply request-id hashing, remove prompt payloads if you prefer, and only include timing attributes and anonymized model metadata. we'll note that in the artifact we send
[07:09] Ivy: timeline check — what can we realistically get by EOW?
[07:14] Ava: Redwood side: filtered traces + request IDs by 2026-05-14, KV metric enablement guide immediately after this call. NovaCommerce side: flow logs and preliminary synthetic run by 2026-05-18. then we reconvene on the 19th for targeted debugging
[07:30] Leah: sounds good. quick thing — we also found some 503s that appeared only when a particular partner service called in a specific header shape; unsure if header size triggers a fallback
[07:42] Julian: interesting, that could be header-parsing path in the gateway. please include an example HTTP header in the follow up so we can repro
[07:50] Marcus: will do. also note our SDK logs show occasional DNS lookups taking 800–1200ms during spikes, maybe unrelated but worth flagging
[07:59] Ava: okay. let's capture that as a lower priority but keep it in the notes.
[08:05] [15:00] short pause for sharing screen and rapid note alignment
[15:20] Julian: switching gears — i want to propose a small test matrix: (1) baseline synthetic in current hosted pool; (2) dedicated small burst pool for 24h; (3) same baseline with increased client pooling + reduced retries. that should isolate whether it's infra saturation, client amplification, or both
[15:38] Rogan: agree. for the dedicated pool test, what's the expected lead time?
[15:42] Ava: we can spin a small dedicated burst pool in 48 hours if approved — costs will be sent in the follow up.
[15:48] Leah: do we need an NDA amendment for dedicated? our legal asked earlier about data residency for dedicated pools
[15:55] Maya: usually no, dedicated burst pools under Redwood Dedicated are in logical isolation; for strict data residency we can discuss Private deployment but that is longer term. we'll loop in legal if needed
[16:06] Ivy: okay wrapping to next steps, I want to confirm action owners and dates
[16:11] Ava: yes summarizing: Julian sends traces & request IDs (due 5/14), Leah shares VPC flow logs & example headers (due 5/15), NovaCommerce runs synthetic baseline and shares results (due 5/18), Ava sends dedicated burst cost delta (due 5/13).
[16:28] Marcus: one operational ask — can Redwood optionally throttle retries at the edge for our route to avoid amplification? even a short circuit that returns a 429 and encourages client to backoff would help
[16:40] Julian: we have route-level backpressure and can apply soft-shedding rules or a lightweight circuit that returns 429 for low-priority routes. that's something we can prototype quickly, though it requires config on both sides to interpret 429s properly
[16:54] Rogan: that may be the lowest-risk mitigate while we investigate root cause
[17:01] Ava: agreed. i'll add that as a short-term mitigation in the notes.
[17:07] Ivy: any blockers for the plan?
[17:10] Leah: only the time to extract and sanitize flow logs, but I can make that a priority this week
[17:15] Maya: Redwood will also redact payloads, so legal should be fine.
[17:19] Ava: great. last procedural item — who should we copy on artifacts?
[17:22] Rogan: copy me, Marcus, Leah and Ivy plus our infra lead (cc: simon@novacomm.com)
[17:29] Ava: noted. thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the zipped trace bundle and the KV metric enablement doc today. next sync proposed 2026-05-19 11am EDT for 30 mins.
[17:39] Marcus: ok thanks
[17:41] Leah: thanks all
[17:42] Ava: bye
